title: Constructors and destructors
objectives: Control what happens when an object is created, copied and destroyed.
Choose between the rule of zero and the rule of five.

screens.title: Last in, first out
screens.question: Put the program's output in order.

hints.text: Both objects live until the closing brace of `main`.
At this brace both are destroyed, one after the other.
They go in reverse order of construction: `b` was built last, so it closes first.

feedback.correct: Built a, b; destroyed b, a.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which object was built last.

byKey.ca: You closed `a` first. Objects are destroyed in reverse order: `b` was built last, so it closes first. `b` might use `a`, so `a` must outlive it.
byKey.w: `work` prints while both objects are alive, before the closing brace.
byKey.cb: Nothing closes until `main` reaches its closing brace, after `work`.

explain.text: Objects are destroyed in reverse order of construction, like plates off a stack. `b` may depend on `a`, so `a` must outlive it. Python gives no such promise about when `__del__` runs; C++ does.

screens.title: Where an object ends
screens.prose: Braces make a **scope**: a block where names live. Here `b` is declared inside an inner pair of braces. Same `Logger` as before.
screens.question: Tap the line where `b`'s destructor runs.

hints.text: Which braces enclose the line that declares `b`?
`b` is declared here.
`b` lives until the closing brace of the block it was declared in.

feedback.correct: `b` dies at the end of its scope, line 6.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the closing brace of the block that declares `b`.

byKey.l5: That is the last line that uses `b`. C++ does not track uses: `b` lives until its scope's closing brace.
byKey.l8: That brace ends `a` and `c`. `b` was declared in the inner block, which ends earlier.
byKey.l4: That line builds `b`. Its destructor runs when its scope ends.
byKey.l7: By line 7 the inner block has already ended, so `b` is gone.

explain.text: An object on the stack lives until the closing brace of its scope. So `b` closes on line 6, before `c` is even built. The rule depends only on the braces, never on when a name was last used.

screens.title: Two scopes
screens.prose: Same program. `c` is built and never used.
screens.question: Put the whole output in order.

hints.text: Walk the lines from top to bottom, printing as each object starts and ends.
Line 6 ends the inner scope.
a, b, work, close b at line 6, then c, and at line 8 close c before close a.

feedback.correct: Each brace ends what it owns, newest first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Walk the lines in order and note every brace that ends a scope.

byKey.oc: `c` is built on line 7, after the inner scope has closed `b`.
byKey.ca: At the last brace both `a` and `c` are alive. `c` was built later, so it closes first.
byKey.cc: `c` is never used, but it is still an object. Its destructor runs at the end of `main`, before `a`'s.

explain.text: Line 6 closes `b`. At line 8 `c` and `a` are both alive, so they close newest first. `c` was never used, yet its constructor and destructor both ran: an object's life follows its scope, not its uses.

screens.title: Produce the order
screens.prose: Now write `Logger` yourself and make a program produce that shape. It reads three names. The first lives for the whole program. The second lives in an inner scope that also prints `work`. The third is built after that scope ends.

This line comes from the destructor of the first logger.
In `main`: `Logger first(x);` then `{ Logger second(y); std::cout << "work\n"; }` then `Logger third(z);`.

feedback.correct: The braces alone decide when each `close` prints.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare your output with the expected lines under the editor.

byKey.compile: The compiler stopped. Check that the destructor is spelt `~Logger()`, with no return type and no arguments.
byKey.test-1: Compare the order of your `close` lines with the expected output. An inner pair of braces must end before `third` is built.

screens.title: Declaration order wins
screens.prose: Members are built in the order they are **declared** in the class, whatever order the initialiser list names them. With `-Wall`, clang warns when the two disagree.

params.title: Terminal
lines: main.cpp:5:21: warning: field 'n_' will be initialized after field 'data_' [-Wreorder-ctor]
main.cpp:5:34: warning: field 'n_' is uninitialized when used here [-Wuninitialized]

screens.question: `Window w(20)` runs. What size does `data_` get?

options.text: Unpredictable: `n_` is read before it is set

options.why: You read the list left to right. `data_` is declared first, so it is built first, from an `n_` not yet set.
An `int` member is not zeroed. Reading it before it is set is undefined behaviour.
These are warnings: the program builds. That is why they are worth reading.

hints.text: Which member is declared first, on lines 7 and 8?
The second warning names the exact problem.
`data_` is built first, using `n_`, which is built second.

feedback.correct: `data_` is built first, from an `n_` that holds garbage.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Members are built in declaration order.

byKey.twenty: You read the list left to right. `data_` is declared first, so it is built first, from an `n_` not yet set.

explain.text: Declaration order decides, so `data_(n_, 0.0)` reads `n_` before `n_(n)` runs. Build `data_` from the parameter, `data_(n, 0.0)`, or declare `n_` first. Keep the list in declaration order and the warning goes away.

screens.title: A copy you did not write
screens.question: How many lines of output start with `close`?

hints.text: How many `Logger` objects exist at the end of `main`?
`b` is a second object holding a copy of `a`'s name.
Two objects, two destructors. The copy itself printed nothing.

feedback.correct: Two objects, so two destructors: `close a` twice.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the objects alive at the closing brace.

byKey.one: You counted one object because only one constructor printed. `b` was built by a constructor that prints nothing, but it still has a destructor.
byKey.three: Only two objects exist. The copy made `b`; it did not make a third.

explain.text: `Logger b = a;` builds `b` with the **copy constructor**, `Logger(const Logger&)`. The compiler wrote one for you: it copies each member and prints nothing. Both objects are destroyed, so `close a` prints twice.

screens.title: Which one runs
screens.prose: A class has four ways to fill an object from another. The **copy constructor** builds a new object. **Copy assignment**, `operator=`, overwrites one that exists. `std::move(a)` marks `a` as finished with, so its contents can be taken: a **move**.
screens.question: Select all that apply: tap every line that runs the copy constructor.

hints.text: Does the line declare a new object, or change one that exists?
On this line `b` already exists.
Lines that declare a new `Buffer` from `a` build it: `Buffer b = a;` and `Buffer c(a);`.

feedback.correct: A declaration builds; a plain `=` overwrites.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether each line makes a new object.

byKey.r3: `b` already exists on this line, so `=` overwrites it: that is copy assignment, not construction.
byKey.r4: `std::move(a)` lets the new object take `a`'s contents: the move constructor runs.
byKey.r5: `c` exists and takes `b`'s contents: move assignment.
byKey.r0: That builds a `Buffer` from two numbers: an ordinary constructor.
byKey.r1: `Buffer b = a;` declares `b`, so it builds a new object. The `=` in a declaration is not assignment, unlike Python.

explain.text: A declaration always builds, even when it is written with `=`. Assignment needs an object that already exists. `std::move` changes which one runs, from copy to move.

screens.title: Copies and moves for free
screens.prose: A `std::vector` member already copies its doubles on a copy and hands over its heap block on a move. So the compiler's versions are right, and `= default` asks for them by name. Declare one special member and the compiler may stop writing the others, so name all four.

rows: copy: b gets its own doubles
move: b takes a's block; a is left empty
copy assignment: b's old doubles give way to copies of a's
move assignment: b takes a's block; a is left empty

screens.question: Write `Buffer(int n, double x)` (n copies of x), `int size() const`, `double get(int i) const`, `void set(int i, double x)`, and the four copy and move members as `= default`.

tests.setup: Buffer a(3, 1.5); Buffer b = a; b.set(0, 9.0);
Buffer a(3, 1.5); Buffer b = a; b.set(0, 9.0);

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 12 hidden tests that copy, move and assign buffers, then read both. One test moves a million doubles.

hints.text: Build `data_` in the initialiser list: `data_(n, x)`.
After a move, the source is left empty.
`Buffer(const Buffer&) = default;`, `Buffer(Buffer&&) = default;`, and `Buffer& operator=(const Buffer&) = default;` with its `Buffer&&` twin. Then write three one-line functions on `data_`.

feedback.correct: The vector did the work; you only asked for it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 changes `b` and reads `a`. A copy must not share doubles with its source.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 reads `a.size()` after a move and expects 0. A moved vector leaves its source empty.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 assigns one buffer to another. A declared move constructor deletes the copy assignment, so default it too.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 moves into an existing buffer. A declared copy constructor stops the compiler writing the move assignment.
byKey.test-12: Test 12 moves `a` into an existing buffer and expects `a` empty. Without a move assignment, `a` was copied.

explain.text: A copy duplicates the doubles; a move passes the heap block over, so a million doubles cost one pointer swap. A moved-from vector is empty; for most other types the standard promises only a valid, unspecified state. Use a moved-from object only to assign it a new value or let it die.

screens.title: Two owners, one block
screens.question: What happens when `main` ends?

options.text: Both destructors `delete[]` the same block: undefined behaviour, which usually crashes a desk build
`b` has its own 100 doubles, so each destructor frees its own
options.why: You expected the copy to copy the doubles. The default copy constructor copies the member, a pointer, so both point at one block.

options.text: A compile error: `Prices` has no copy constructor
options.why: The compiler writes one for you. It copies each member, and for a pointer that copies the address.

options.text: The block leaks, because nobody frees it
options.why: Each destructor frees it, so it is freed twice, not never.

hints.text: What is the member that the default copy copies?
Draw the arrow for `b` after the copy.
`data_` is an address. `b` gets the same address, so two destructors free one block.

feedback.correct: Copying a raw pointer copies an address, not the doubles.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the default copy does with `data_`.

byKey.deep: You expected the copy to copy the doubles. The default copy constructor copies the member, a pointer, so both point at one block.

explain.text: `b.data_` holds the same address as `a.data_`, so the block is freed twice. The fix is to own it with a member that manages itself: `std::vector<double>` copies properly, and `std::unique_ptr<double[]>` refuses to copy. Then the class needs no destructor at all.

screens.title: The rule of zero
screens.question: A `Pricer` holds `std::string name_` and `std::unique_ptr<Lattice> grid_`. What do you write for copying, moving and destruction?

options.text: Nothing. Copies are refused because `unique_ptr` cannot be copied, and moves work.
All five special members, by hand
options.why: That is for a class that owns a raw resource itself. Here every member already manages its own.
`unique_ptr` already deletes the lattice. Deleting it again is a double delete.

options.text: A copy constructor that copies the pointer
options.why: Two pricers would then share one lattice, and both would try to delete it.

hints.text: Does any member need help to be copied, moved or destroyed?
`std::string` and `std::unique_ptr` each handle their own copying, moving and destruction.

feedback.correct: Rule of zero: the members already do the right thing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check what each member does on its own.

explain.text: Self-managing members make the compiler's versions right: moves move, and the copy is deleted because `unique_ptr` cannot be copied. Write the five only when the class itself holds a raw resource. `= delete` says a copy makes no sense.

screens.title: A connection that disconnects once
screens.prose: A market-data connection must disconnect exactly once, in its destructor. A copy would disconnect twice, so copying is deleted. It may be moved, say out of a factory. The new object takes over, and the old one must be left closed so its destructor does nothing.

state.caption: After the move, only `b` is open.

screens.question: Write the destructor, delete copying, and write the move constructor so that each venue is disconnected exactly once.

tests.setup: { Connection a("LSE"); Connection b = std::move(a); Connection c = std::move(b); }

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 9 hidden tests. Hidden code counts calls to `disconnect` in `disconnects`; two tests ask whether `Connection` can be copied or moved.

hints.text: The destructor calls `disconnect(venue_)` only while `open_` is true.
After the move, `a` must be closed.
`Connection(Connection&& other) noexcept : venue_(std::move(other.venue_)), open_(other.open_) { other.open_ = false; }` and `Connection(const Connection&) = delete;`.

feedback.correct: One open connection, one disconnect, wherever it moves.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test under the editor.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 moves `a` into `b`; both destructors run. Leave `other.open_` false in the move constructor.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 asks whether `Connection` can be copied. Write `Connection(const Connection&) = delete;`.
byKey.test-1: Test 1 builds one connection and expects one disconnect. Call `disconnect(venue_)` in `~Connection()` while it is open.

explain.text: The move constructor takes the venue and closes the source, so only one destructor disconnects. Deleting the copy turns a double disconnect into a compile error. A pricer's lattice works the same way: returned from a factory by move, its buffer is handed over, never copied.

ideas: A destructor runs when its object's scope ends, in reverse order of construction. A temporary dies at the end of its full expression. Members are built in declaration order.
`T b = a;` builds `b` with the copy constructor; `b = a;` on an existing `b` is copy assignment. `std::move(a)` lets a new object take `a`'s contents.
Rule of zero: hold members that manage themselves (`std::vector`, `std::string`, `std::unique_ptr`) and write no special members. Owning a raw resource needs all five, or `= delete`.

formula.name: Order of destruction
formula.tex: \text{built } a, b, c \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{destroyed } c, b, a
formula.note: Within one scope, newest first; an inner scope ends at its own closing brace.

summary.trap: A class holding a raw pointer gets a default copy that copies the address, so two destructors free one block. Hold a `std::vector` or `std::unique_ptr` instead.

quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: A temporary has no name, so it does not live to the end of the scope. It dies at the end of its full expression, the `;`.
The temporary is really built, so both its constructor and its destructor run.
Every object that is built is destroyed. The temporary's destructor runs at the `;`.

feedback.correct: A temporary dies at the end of its full expression.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A temporary has no scope of its own.

explain.text: `Logger("tmp");` builds an unnamed object and destroys it at the semicolon. So `close tmp` prints before `next`. A reference to a temporary's insides dangles for the same reason.

quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: `std::move` only casts. On a `const` object it gives `const Buffer&&`, which the move constructor cannot take, so the copy constructor runs.

options.text: A compile error: you cannot move from a `const` object
options.why: It compiles. The copy constructor accepts a `const` object, so the compiler quietly picks it.

feedback.correct: A `const` object cannot be moved from, so it is copied.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A move must change its source.

explain.text: A move empties its source, and `a` is `const`, so the copy constructor runs instead. `a` keeps its 3 doubles. Do not mark an object `const` if you plan to move it.

quiz.question: How many times are the 500 doubles copied?

options.why: You expected `return grid;` to copy. A returned local is moved, or built straight into `g`.
Neither the return nor `Lattice g = ...` copies. C++17 builds `g` straight from the returned value.

feedback.correct: Returning a local by value never copies it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A returned local is moved or built in place.

explain.text: The compiler usually builds `grid` directly in `g`'s place; if not, it moves it. Either way no double is copied. So return big objects by value: no pointer or out-parameter needed.

quiz.question: Which line prints first?

options.why: You followed the initialiser list. Members are built in declaration order, and `risk_` is declared first.
Nothing closes until `d` is destroyed at the end of `main`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the order of the member declarations.

explain.text: `risk_` is declared first, so it is built first, whatever the list says. At the end the order reverses: `close feed`, then `close risk`.
